items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    This work aims to investigate the formation processes of the charcoal assemblage from level Ra at Abric Romaní, a well-preserved Middle Palaeolithic rock shelter in north-eastern Spain that was occupied by Neanderthals. To this end, we adopted an anthracological approach that combines both taxonomic and taphonomic observations. Spatial patterns and potential formation processes were explored through spatial analysis using Kernel Density Estimation and the Moran’s index across the excavated layer. These analyses were performed using the Cartesian coordinates of the archaeological charcoal fragments recovered in the level and included their taxonomic identification and documented taphonomic modifications. The correlations between alterations were also tested to identify possible interactions among the phenomena that affected the charcoal fragments. Finally, we integrated these findings with data from other previously studied archaeological levels in the archaeological sequence. Our findings, contextualized at the beginning of MIS 3, indicate a dominance of
                    <jats:italic>Pinus sylvestris</jats:italic>
                    , indicating the continuity of well-established mountain pine forests at elevations below their current boundary. Our taphonomic observations suggest low to moderate postdepositional processes affecting specific areas of the rock shelter, mainly related to small waterflows. After controlling for different taphonomic processes, differences in charcoal fragment distributions between the northern and southern sectors suggest distinct human activities, which are interpreted as signs of differences in use and potentially representing waste-management events. The results suggest the potential of integrating spatial studies of archaeological charcoal fragments in order to gain valuable insights into hearth-related assemblage formation.
                  </jats:p>

items.abstract: <jats:p>The distribution and abundance of species is a product of the interplay of climatic and environmental factors, both past and present, natural, and anthropogenic. In the most recent stage of the Anthropocene, these changes have been extremely rapid and abrupt. The objective of this work is to discuss some socio-environmental problems of northern Patagonia by comparing micromammal archeological and paleontological sequences attributable to the final Late-Holocene and post-Hispanic period with current samples from the region. Several sites in northern Patagonia, from the Andean forest, the Steppe and Monte regions, and their ecotone, were selected as study cases. The comparison of the species composition from the final Late-Holocene and post-Hispanic assemblages with local small mammal communities indicates species extinctions, considerable reductions in their distributional ranges, and an increase in the abundance of opportunistic taxa. The causes have been attributed to the accelerated deterioration of natural ecosystems due to anthropogenic factors, including habitat destruction caused by the expansion of agriculture and livestock farming, the introduction of exotic plant and animal species, soil compaction, and other factors. Paleoecology, as a historical science of nature, inevitably requires the use of modern analogues in its interpretations, a situation that became increasingly difficult and challenging in the times of the Anthropocene, where current communities are constantly changing due to anthropogenic causes.</jats:p>

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Research on Palaeolithic bone tools has increasingly emphasised methodological refinement and interdisciplinary approaches, yet systematic quantitative assessments of scholarly attention and bias remain limited. This study presents a quantitative synthesis of 137 publications aimed at analysing patterns in tool-type focus, geographic coverage, and methodological change in European Palaeolithic bone-tool research. Within the Middle Palaeolithic context, retouchers emerge as the continuously foregrounded discrete category, while other artefact categories, often characterised by subtler traces or more ambiguous manufacturing and use traces, remain marginal. Using descriptive statistics, Fisher’s exact tests, and logistic regression, we identify a pronounced and persistent attention bias: retouchers constitute a dominant focus and are more likely to be analysed with functional methods (use-wear, experimentation, 3D imaging). Geographically, research is heavily concentrated in Western Europe, with France and Italy accounting for nearly half of all studies, while Spain shows a distinct association with retoucher-focused work. Temporally, we document a measurable shift from typological description toward techno-functional and interdisciplinary analysis, a trend that is statistically significant but unevenly distributed across tool types and regions. These findings underscore how research priorities, validation strategies, and regional academic traditions shape the archaeological narrative of early bone technology. Over time, this imbalance may narrow reconstructions of Palaeolithic bone technology toward activities closely aligned with lithic production, inadvertently downplaying other domains of bone use such as hide processing, plant working, composite tool manufacture, or percussive tasks unrelated to stone-tool maintenance. The issue is therefore not simply one of bias, but of epistemic filtering: certain behaviours become more visible because they align with dominant validation strategies, while others remain under-represented. We argue that future studies should extend high-resolution functional analyses beyond retouchers, broaden geographic and chronological representation, and adopt more standardised reporting to advance a more balanced understanding of Palaeolithic bone-tool behaviours.</jats:p>

items.title: Retouchers at the centre: quantifying attention bias and methodological change in middle palaeolithic bone-tool research in Europe

items.abstract: Northeast China and Russian Primorye lie at the confluence of the East Asian summer monsoon, Siberian High, and Pacific maritime circulation. The region experienced pronounced glacial-interglacial variability and served as a corridor for human dispersal among Siberia, East Asia, and the Americas. This review synthesises palaeoecological and archaeological evidence, principally from the past ca. 50 ka. Environmental records trace a transition from the cold, arid steppe of the Last Glacial Maximum (ca. 26.5–19.0 ka BP) to warmer, more forested Holocene landscapes, while revealing strong spatial heterogeneity and abrupt events. Although the ≥146 ka Harbin cranium predates the main review interval, it establishes a Middle Pleistocene hominin presence; securely dated archaeological sequences considered here begin in the Late Pleistocene. These records document developments from Upper Palaeolithic lithic industries to Neolithic sedentism, millet agriculture, and Bronze Age sociopolitical complexity. A central limitation is the spatial separation of most palaeoclimatic archives and archaeological sites. Their differing chronological resolution further restricts direct causal attribution, leaving many proposed climate-culture relationships as working hypotheses. We therefore advocate co-located multiproxy transects, improved chronological control, and tephrochronological correlation. A site-by-site appraisal of radiocarbon, OSL, and U-series chronologies identifies relationships that are currently testable. The Boisman-Krounovka sequence suggests that resource breadth and specialisation may mediate vulnerability to environmental change, although the roles of social organisation, mobility, and demography remain unresolved. Northeast Asia thus offers a framework for generating and testing hypotheses about climatic variability, demographic processes, and cultural change rather than demonstrating simple climate-driven causation.

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    This study presents the first detailed description of bioerosion traces produced by insects in bones from the Santa Cruz Sequence (early Carnian, Santa Maria Supersequence, Brazil). An array of traces is reported, consisting of notches, a tube, trails of grooves attributed to the ichnotaxon
                    <jats:italic>Osteocallis mandibulus</jats:italic>
                    and ornamented depressions attributed to a new ichnotaxon
                    <jats:italic>Osteograptus thanatobios</jats:italic>
                    igen. nov. et isp. nov. The traces were likely produced by insects, but a less inclusive taxonomic attribution is currently not possible. The ethological interpretation for the bioerosion structures is that they represent feeding traces. This report increases the contrast between the Middle and Late Triassic bioerosion record, since the latter is significantly more diverse and abundant. Hypotheses related to the onset of the Carnian Humid Episode as well as taphonomic biases are discussed as possible explanations for this contrast.
                  </jats:p>

items.abstract:
<jats:p>
                    The Arctic is warming faster than any other region on Earth. As sea ice diminishes, the surface boundary conditions, such as roughness and air–sea coupling, change and open‐water fetch increases. This may enhance wind forcing on Arctic coasts. Lake sediments can record these changes through the deposition of wind‐blown grains and elements, offering insights into past wind and climate dynamics. We reconstruct
                    <jats:italic>c</jats:italic>
                    . 8200 years of wind and climate variability using laminated sediments from a closed‐basin lake in central Spitsbergen, Svalbard archipelago, High Arctic. By integrating geochemical, visual and granulometric fingerprints within a multiproxy geostatistical framework, we link aeolian minerogenic input to specific catchment sources. Our findings show that iron (Fe)‐rich coarse silt‐sized clasts originate from distinct dolerite outcrops west and northwest of the lake, upwind of the dominant summer westerlies. This reveals a locally filtered westerly input that aligns with valley‐fjord channelling. We identify four phases of enhanced aeolian activity during the Mid‐ and Late Holocene, which occurred when local boundary conditions were favourable for entraining and transporting sediment into the basin. Major shifts in sediment sources and depositional conditions coincide with the end of the Holocene Thermal Maximum and the gradual onset of the Neoglacial. However, the reconstructed wind signal demonstrates a comparatively stable long‐term behaviour, with no clear correspondence to regional palaeoclimate records.
                  </jats:p>
authors: Willem G. M. van der Bilt
